prerequisites: Basic mathematics, as required to pass the OFA test.

learning_outcomes.text: Provide basic knowledge in the field of linear algebra (analysis of linear systems, matrix reduction and decomposition into structurally simple forms, aimed at applications) and analytic geometry (geometric interpretation of equations).
Use the language of linear algebra to describe linear phenomena in the field of analytic geometry.
Knowledge of mathematical principles and understanding of the role of the mathematical sciences as a tool for the analysis and solution of problems and models underlying industrial engineering.
Understanding of the broader multidisciplinary context of engineering.
Ability to apply mathematical methods—particularly those related to geometry and linear algebra—to model, analyze, and solve engineering problems.

Ability to combine theory and practice to solve multidisciplinary engineering problems and to contribute to the implementation of engineering projects, working collaboratively with engineers and non-engineers.
Ability to analyze data and information using established methods and tools, interpret the results, and draw consistent conclusions, also with the support of provided guidance.

Ability to organize one's own work in compliance with assigned commitments and deadlines, managing the available time and resources, realistically assessing one's own capabilities, and contributing to the prioritization of activities.
Ability to recognize one's own knowledge limitations and the need to acquire new competences, identifying appropriate information sources and guided learning opportunities.
Ability to present problems, solutions, analyses, and results clearly and in a structured manner through written reports and oral presentations, according to standard formats and procedures.
Ability to represent and communicate data, results, and technical solutions graphically through the preparation of diagrams, graphs, and tables, using established tools and conventions.

Ability to identify and consult bibliographic sources and technical documentation through the main available resources (libraries, databases, manuals, and digital sources), selecting relevant information with the support of provided guidance.

Knowledge of the principles of mathematics and an understanding of the role of mathematical sciences as tools for analysing and solving problems and modelling the phenomena underlying industrial engineering, with particular reference to mechanical engineering. Knowledge of the principles of computer science and of the algorithmic and numerical approaches to problem solving.

Ability to apply mathematical methods—particularly differential and integral calculus, geometry, linear algebra, numerical methods, probability, and statistics—to model, analyse, and solve engineering problems, also using appropriate computational tools.

syllabus_topics: Vectors, operations on vectors. Scalar product, vector product, triple product. Vector spaces, linear dependence, basis, dimension. Subspaces and their operations. Numerical vector spaces.
Linear systems: Matrices. Operations on matrices and properties, special matrices. Determinant, rank. Linear systems of equations. Solutions of linear systems. Gauss Elimination Method.
Linear analytic geometry: Parametric and Cartesian equations for subspaces. Lines, planes. Parallelism and perpendicularity.
Linear metric geometry: Scalar products. Distance, angle, area, volume.

Linear maps, Kernel and image. Projections and orthogonal projections. Matrices associated to linear maps. Change of basis. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Diagonalization. Diagonalization of symmetric matrices and spectral theorem.
Vector spaces: Vectors, operations on vectors. Generated subspaces, linear dependence, basis, dimension. Numerical vector spaces. Scalar product, vector product, triple product.
Linear metric geometry: Scalar products. Distance, angle, area, volume. Ortoghonal projection.

Linear maps: Linear transformations. Kernel and image. Matrices associated to linear maps. Change of basis. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Diagonalization. Diagonalization of symmetric matrices and spectral theorem. Applications related to conics.
teaching_methods: Texts of written examinations from previous years
assessment_rules: The final evaluation is based on a written and oral exam. Each written exam consists of 11 questions on the topics of the course. The teacher may not require the oral part, which, however, remains optional for the student. The student is expected to demonstrate a basic knowledge of the topics and be able to apply it in problem solving. Grading criteria are given for Fail, 18-22 (Sufficient), 23-25 (Satisfactory), 26-28 (Good or very good), and 29-30 and Honors (Excellent or outstanding).
